mark_breakdown.desc: Applying product rule and chain rule to $(\sin x)e^{\cos x}$
Factoring out the common exponential term

subparts.solution:
$\frac{d}{dx}((\sin x)e^{\cos x}) = (\cos x)e^{\cos x} + (\sin x)((-\sin x)e^{\cos x}) \quad \{\text{product rule}\}$
$= (\cos x)e^{\cos x} - (\sin^2 x)e^{\cos x}$
$= e^{\cos x}(\cos x - \sin^2 x)$

ai_explanation.concept_rule: Combination of product rule and chain rule: $\frac{d}{dx}(e^{\cos x}) = -\sin x \cdot e^{\cos x}$.
step_by_step: Compute $u' = \cos x$ and $v' = -\sin x \cdot e^{\cos x}$.
Combine terms: $u'v + uv' = \cos x e^{\cos x} - \sin^2 x e^{\cos x}$.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Sign error when differentiating $\cos x$ in the exponent.
